item.title: Extremity in Organisations: Conceptualising and Managing the Spectrum of Extreme Conditions
item.content:encoded:
Xi Wen (Carys) Chan, Griffith University

Shea Fan, Deakin University

Graham Dwyer, The University of Dublin

Margaret A. Shaffer, University of Oklahoma

Contemporary organisations increasingly face conditions of extremity, from acute crises and disasters to the mundane extremity embedded in everyday operations. While existing research examines extreme events in specific contexts, there is a lack of conceptual foundations understanding how extremity manifests, evolves, and impacts organisations holistically beyond extreme contexts research.

This special issue aims to consolidate knowledge across human resource management, psychology, organisational behaviour and other fields to develop frameworks for understanding extremity from different standpoints with different disciplines. The issue will establish extremity as an emerging domain of inquiry to provide conceptual foundations with practical implications for managing high-stakes environments.

Appel publié par Personnel Review. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Conceptualising extremity in an organisational context - theoretical clarity to the construct of extremity, attributes that render phenomena extreme, boundaries of extremity, diverse theoretical perspectives, equivocality and its effects on individuals and groups, ambiguity and improvisation, sensemaking in breached or disrupted circumstances
  • Processes or mechanisms that organisations use to cope with extremity - individual and group responses, adaptation in the moment, improvisation as catalyst for transformation, theoretical understanding of coping, adjustment and organisational transformation in face of extremity
  • The impact of extremity on individuals - cognition, behaviour, embodied reactions, wellbeing and performance under extremity, individual coping mechanisms, novel sensemaking and leverage of challenges
  • Conceptualising extremity in occupational contexts - distinctive manifestations across occupational domains, extremity as part of everyday and mundane contexts, occupational-specific theoretical understanding
  • Extremity caused by advanced technologies - relationship between technology and extremity, technological change reshaping work intensity and performance, AI and innovation effects, blurred boundaries between extreme and normal

Timeline

  • January 30, 2026: Closing date for abstract submission
  • September 30, 2026: Closing date for manuscripts submission

item.title: Navigating the Work–Family Interface in the Digital Era: Challenges and Strategies
item.content:encoded:
The rapid digitalization of work—driven by advances in information and communication technologies, remote and hybrid work arrangements, and GenAI-enabled systems—has fundamentally reshaped the boundaries between work and family domains. While digital tools provide unprecedented flexibility and autonomy, they also blur temporal and spatial boundaries, intensify role demands, and generate new forms of work–family conflict. This transformation is especially salient in knowledge-intensive and digitally-mediated work contexts, where the 'always-on' culture may foster constant connectivity, hinder psychological detachment, and undermine employee well-being and family functioning. At the same time, digitalization presents important opportunities for work–family enrichment. Flexible work arrangements and hybrid models can enhance individuals' capacity to integrate work and family roles, consistent with resource-based perspectives on the work–home interface. However, these benefits are not evenly distributed. item.title: Toward a Human-Centered Workplace: Empowering Diversity and Inclusion in the Age of Artificial Intelligence
item.content:encoded:
This Special Issue aims to advance understanding of how AI is reshaping work and employment for underrepresented groups, and to stimulate research on how HRM can foster more inclusive, equitable, and human-centered AI-enabled workplaces. It seeks to bring together multidisciplinary scholarship examining both the opportunities and risks of AI for women, migrants, refugees, older workers, people with disabilities, and Indigenous employees. These aims will be met by inviting conceptual, empirical, and review-based contributions that examine bias, accessibility, trust, human–AI collaboration, inclusive design, and responsible governance in AI-HRM systems. In doing so, the Special Issue will generate new theoretical insights, practical implications, and future research directions that position HRM scholarship to respond more effectively to the challenges and possibilities of AI-driven organizational change, while helping organizations foster more equitable, inclusive, and human-centered human–AI interactions.

Appel publié par Personnel Review. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • AI in Talent Acquisition and Selection: How do AI-based recruitment and selection systems create, reproduce, or mitigate biases against candidates from underrepresented groups (e.g., people with disabilities, older workers, migrants), and what mechanisms can ensure equitable outcomes in AI-assisted hiring?
  • Accessibility and Inclusion in Employment: In what ways can AI technologies be designed to enhance workplace accessibility, enable equitable participation, and expand employment opportunities for employees with disabilities or other marginalized groups?
  • Human–AI Collaboration and Bias Mitigation: How can human oversight, input from minority employees, and inclusive design processes help AI systems learn more equitably—reducing bias and performing more human-like or human-better tasks in HR contexts?
  • Talent Development, Reskilling, and Learning in the Age of AI: How can HRM leverage AI-enabled learning, development, and reskilling systems to support diverse employees and prepare both workers and organizations for ethical AI use? How can organizations use talent development strategies to train both humans and AI systems toward ethical and inclusive performance?
  • Ethical, Legal, and Governance Challenges in AI-HRM: What are the ethical and legal implications of using AI in managing diversity and disability inclusion, and how can organizations establish responsible AI governance frameworks aligned with human rights and DEI principles?

Timeline

  • January 9, 2026: Opening date for manuscripts submissions
  • January 3, 2027: Closing date for manuscripts submission
